summary: Extends MPLS LSP Ping and traceroute so they can test pseudowires whose forwarding equivalence classes are advertised over IPv6, which the earlier specifications did not cover. It was replaced by RFC 8029.

eli5.summary: A way to check whether a delivery tunnel works now also understands the newer style of address on the tunnel's label.

subtitle: Testing pseudowires that use IPv6 addresses with label switched path ping and traceroute

tldr.problem: The LSP Ping and traceroute mechanisms (RFC 4379) for testing MPLS pseudowires only worked with IPv4 addresses; networks using IPv6 LDP sessions could not test their pseudowires.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6829 extends the existing pseudowire FEC sub-TLVs to be explicitly IPv4-only and defines two new sub-TLVs for IPv6 pseudowires (FEC 128 and FEC 129), allowing the same testing mechanisms to work with IPv6.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now detect and isolate data-plane failures in pseudowires set up over IPv6 LDP sessions. This RFC was superseded by RFC 8029.

today: This RFC was superseded by RFC 8029, which consolidated the LSP Ping mechanisms and added support for additional MPLS applications beyond just IPv4 and IPv6 pseudowires. RFC 8029 is the current standard for LSP Ping and Traceroute.

sections.title: The Problem
sections.content:
MPLS Label Switched Path (LSP) Ping and traceroute, defined in RFC 4379, are standard mechanisms for detecting and isolating data-plane failures in MPLS Label Switched Paths (LSPs), including those used for pseudowires.

However, the pseudowire LSP Ping and traceroute mechanisms were not specified for IPv6 address usage. The existing pseudowire Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) sub-TLVs could only carry IPv4 addresses. When an IPv6 LDP session is used to set up and maintain a pseudowire, the existing sub-TLVs cannot represent the Sender's and Receiver's PE addresses because they are 16 octets each (IPv6), not 4 octets (IPv4).
sections.eli5: A tunnel testing tool was built to work with the old-style IPv4 addresses. When people started using the new IPv6 addresses, the tool did not know what to do.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6 FEC Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
RFC 6829 clarifies and extends the pseudowire FEC sub-TLVs. The existing three sub-TLVs from RFC 4379 are renamed to explicitly indicate they carry IPv4 addresses: FEC 128 Pseudowire - IPv4 (Deprecated), FEC 128 Pseudowire - IPv4, and FEC 129 Pseudowire - IPv4. The names change, but the actual structures and semantics do not change; the renaming merely clarifies their use.

Two new sub-TLVs are defined for IPv6: FEC 128 Pseudowire - IPv6 (Type 24) and FEC 129 Pseudowire - IPv6 (Type 25). These have the same structure as their IPv4 counterparts but use 16-octet fields for the Sender's PE IPv6 Address and Remote PE IPv6 Address.
sections.eli5: The old tool has two versions: one labeled "IPv4" (the original) and one labeled "IPv6" (the new one). Each version understands the right address style.

sections.title: FEC 128 Pseudowire IPv6 Structure
sections.content:
The FEC 128 Pseudowire IPv6 sub-TLV (Type 24) contains a 16-octet Sender's PE IPv6 Address, a 16-octet Remote PE IPv6 Address, a 4-octet PW ID, and a 2-octet PW Type field (with a 2-octet Must Be Zero field). The total length is 38 octets.

The Sender's PE IPv6 Address is the source IP address of the target IPv6 LDP session. The Remote PE IPv6 Address is the destination IP address of the target IPv6 LDP session. The PW ID and PW Type are the same as in the IPv4 version.
sections.eli5: The IPv6 version of the tunnel identifier packet has two IPv6 addresses (32 octets total) plus information about the tunnel type and ID.

sections.title: FEC 129 Pseudowire IPv6 Structure
sections.content: The FEC 129 Pseudowire IPv6 sub-TLV (Type 25) is structured similarly to FEC 128 but adds Attachment Group Identifier (AGI), Source Attachment Individual Identifier (SAII), and Target Attachment Individual Identifier (TAII) fields to support virtual circuit identification. It contains 16-octet Sender's PE IPv6 Address and Remote PE IPv6 Address fields, followed by PW Type and the attachment identifiers. The total length is 40 octets plus the variable-length attachment fields, with padding to a multiple of 4 octets.
sections.eli5: The FEC 129 version is like FEC 128 but includes extra fields to identify which specific virtual connection the tunnel carries.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: RFC 6829 does not define new procedures; the operation described in RFC 4379 MUST be used. An operator or automated tool runs LSP Ping or traceroute on a pseudowire. If the pseudowire uses IPv6 LDP sessions, the tool uses the new IPv6 FEC sub-TLVs (Type 24 or 25) in the Target FEC Stack to identify the pseudowire. The network devices receiving the ping or traceroute message understand these new types and can process the request.
sections.eli5: The technician uses the same testing tool as before, but the tool now knows how to speak about IPv6 tunnels.

sections.title: IANA and Standards
sections.content: IANA assigned Type values 24 and 25 for the two new IPv6 FEC sub-TLVs in the MPLS Label Switched Paths Ping Parameters registry. The three existing IPv4 sub-TLVs (Types 9, 10, 11) retain their assignments but are now clarified as IPv4-specific.
sections.eli5: The IANA registry (the official list of protocol numbers) now lists both the IPv4 versions and the IPv6 versions of the tunnel identifier types.
